newsitem.title: THAILAND: Economic moves may keep Chavalit in power - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Economic moves may keep Chavalit in power - analysts.

text.p: Thailand's decision to seek help from the International Monetary Fund to get the economy back on track may end up helping premier Chavalit Yongchaiyudh keep his job, at least for a while, analysts said on Wednesday.

Help from the IMF in setting economic measures coupled with a reform of the political system could show the public Chavalit is willing to take the toughest decisions to put the economy and the country back on track, they said.
But Thailand's two English-language newspapers on Wednesday angrily pointed the finger of blame at Chavalit, with one calling on him to quit.

Chavalit's eight-month old, six-party coalition government is struggling to end the country's worst economic crisis in over a decade. On the political front it has faced strong pressure to accept a new constitution revamping the political structure and ending rampant money politics.
The premier said last week he would do his best to get the constitution passed in order to avoid unrest.
The coalition had previously hinted it may not accept the constitution because it proposed reforms that could limit support of parties like Chavalit's New Aspiration Party.
In addition, Chavalit opposed a proposal in the new charter that would force all cabinet ministers to be non-elected.

Amid the economic and political uncertainty there have been rumours over the past two weeks that the military, which engineered 17 successful or attempted coups since a change from absolute monarchy in 1932, may stage another putsch.

"This vulnerable government has been facing both an economic and political crisis, so it has been forced to defuse two bombs," Somjai Pagaphagvivat, an economist and political science lecturer at Thammasat University, told Reuters.
"The first issue has already begun to be solved by accepting the conditions of the IMF. The IMF is regarded as a new hope for the people," he said.
The government on Tuesday announced a series of tough monetary and fiscal measures as recommended by the IMF, with the hope of obtaining up to $15 billion in loans from the IMF and foreign nations.
Some of the measures, like the suspension of over half the country's finance firms and a three percentage point hike in value added tax, were hard to swallow.
"It was a shock but inevitable," Somjai said. "IMF measures are the toughest ones. It's like a doctor who performs surgery that's painful but needed."
Sukhum Naulsakul, political science lecturer at Ramkhamheang University, said that the dire economic situation would likely force Chavalit to accept political reform.

"Chavalit seems to be aware that unqualified politicians and money politicking is what is responsible for the economic downfall, so reforming the politics to have better qualified politicians is inevitable," Sukhum told Reuters.
"The new charter is another new hope for the nation, apart from the IMF, and if the government refuses the new constitution its would risk public unrest," Sukhum said.
The 99-member Constitution Drafting Assembly (CDA) has been working for the past eight months. It will put the draft before parliament for approval later this month.
The 393 members of the lower house and 262 appointed senators are to vote on the new charter by early September.
"People hope that once the charter is approved this government will go within two years and they can expect fresh and better politicians," Sukhum said.

Chavalit, whose coalition commands 222 of the lower house seats, vowed in November to dissolve his government within two years to organise new polls in accordance with a new charter. He repeated this promise last week.
The military said they would vote for the new constitution even though some generals were not satisfied with the draft, which curbs military power in the political arena.
"Most of the military senators are expected to vote for the new constitution, otherwise we will be blamed for causing more public unrest," an army officer told Reuters.

The English-language Bangkok Post and The Nation newspapers slated the country's leaders for bringing the once-booming economy to its lowest growth level in a decade and forcing it to seek aid from the IMF.

"Let's not forget how this country wound up in this sorry debacle in the first place," said the Bangkok Post. "Politicians of all shades -- including General Chavalit -- are to blame. They have allowed this country to surrender its economic sovereignty because of their gross mismanagement over the past several years."
The Nation called on Chavalit, who has had two finance ministers and two central bank governors in his eight months in office, to step down soon.
"There is little Chavalit can do or show that will make anyone think he can do better than he has."
